review:
Youngblood's premise is one of those ideas that must have been easy to get the stakeholders to buy into: A Wolfenstein game with coop. When you then hear that it is a collaboration between MachineGames and Arkane, it looks like even more of a slam-dunk, two studios known for their work on games with a good mix of stealth and gory action.

Unfortunately, it doesn't quite come together. 

The things that work are truly excellent: the environments are beautiful and the more non-linear level design clearly show the influence from Arkane Studios. The game works well as a coop (I only played coop), and things like the peps are a nice way to support your partner. The weapon customization is a pretty neat aspect, but not that impactful and the kind of stealth they are trying to emphasize is really hampered by the lack of a proper sniper rifle. The storyline is fine, if a bit predictable, and I think the cringy mood of the two protagonists work in the naturally cringy 80's setting. The price also feels reasonable and the Buddy-pass is a nice inclusion, even though it probably should just have been included in the base game.

On the negative side, the 'progression' system is obviously at the top of the list. It feels unnecessary and doesn't seem to serve any actual porpose in gameplay, apart from a skinnerbox 'ding' sound whenever you level. The light/heavy armor system also ends up as a drag on the rest of the game, because it basically fixes a problem that did not exist. I don't want to have to juggle my weapons with the somewhat bulky inventory management system, just because the enemy I happen to be fighting does not understand that a hundred bullets from my dual machine pistols is supposed to kill him. Also, enough elevators already! And can you please just open the doors with a button instead of forcing them open EVERY time, that animation gets really dull after the first 20 times. And a last couple of quibbles: why do I have to take a perk to dual-wield and why can I only dual-wield the pistols? This was one of THE things The New Order fixed. And what the hell is up with that boss-fight at the end?

This is one of those games where I wish I had a 'meh', a thumb-between-up-and-down on the recommendation. I don't, so I simply have to conclude that the negative outweigh the positive and say that no, I would not recommend Wolfenstein: Youngblood.

This game has been marketed as Wolfenstein with a friend. Why not just make that? Look at the screenshots and videos. Beautiful graphics, tight controls, satisfying gory combat with a friend. It's simple but looks like great fun.

But instead, enemies have fucking RPG floating health bars. Some basic common enemies are so bullet spongey they take multiple mags to bring down while you kite them around. Bosses are the same story but on steroids.

On top of that, you can only do missions that you're the right level for, otherwise if you try to progress beyond a certain point the enemies will be absurdly strong and one shot you. One bullet will take you from max health to zero. And they're not special enemies or anything, they're the same grunts you've been killing already but with a skull by their health bar. 

Why add RPG / looter shooter mechanics into an excellent fps game? Just why?

Wolfenstein Youngblood has the following features:
-A story that makes no sense at all
-Extremely annoying characters
-Around 3(!!!) or so unique missions, the rest being a hub-world that you grind for hours
-Six very small maps that you need to run through and cleanse over and over again, for mundane fetch quests
-Enemies respawning as soon as you turn your back (not exaggerating)
-A damage system that forces you to use specific weapons without the system making any sense
-Level-gated enemies that are impossible to defeat until you grind enough so your weapons magically start dealing more damage
-A stealth system that is so bare-bones that you'll be forgiven for not noticing it exists in the first place
-Microtransactions
-Unplayable singleplayer due to some of the worst friendly AI in the history of gaming

Overall, very little content, no variety, frustrating gameplay mechanics and other woeful creative decisions. It's lazy, cynical and shameless. The game is a mess. And the more you think about it, the more you start to realize that Younblood falls in line with Bethesda's modern approach to game production. It's obvious just how much of an influence Bethesda had on the development of this game. Fallout 76, Rage 2 and now this. It isn't just a coincidence that three different games from three different developers just happened to come out very similar.

Don't buy it. Even at a sale.

This game is emblematic of everything that is wrong with Bethesda these days. It is an unplayably broken mess of an attempt to cash in on one of their well known and historically good franchises, which uses the brand name to suck players in, then delivers nothing of the content they would expect, and has the audacity to nickle and dime them with microtransactions the whole way through. It's lazy, dishonest, and frankly insulting to their customers.

Wolfenstein Youngblood has nothing in common with the previous two entries in the series, which were both good games. They have ditched the chaotic, ultra-violent combat and action of the previous two games, for a hybrid shooter/RPG forced co-op style of gameplay. The result is that there is no true single player mode, and even when playing offline, you'll be forced to play co-op with the game's horrendous AI. There are 2 person gimmicks such as activating levers in two seperate rooms simultaniously to open a door, which get incredibly old very quickly, and a revive system that ruins the pace of combat. Enemies are level gated with healthbars and effectivly become bullet sponges at higher levels. Speaking of which, ammo is scarce and you don't get it back if you die and have to respawn, meaning you may have to fight through the entire level all over again if you die at the end of a level with no ammo. 

Did I mention ammo was scarce? Not to worry! Your pals at Bethesda have  "gold bars" you can buy through steam with your real money, and you can pay to get more! You can buy skins for your character you can't even see while playing for the most part! You can buy skins for your guns! Upgrades to get through the bullet sponge enemies! Abilities and perks to level up your character! How great is that? Thanks, Bethesda!

The story is cringey, the characters are obnoxious and unlikable, and there's an audio bug that distorts the sound during combat, rendering the game essentially unplayable, that was supposed to be fixed 7 months ago, and still hasn't been. There is no reason anyone should buy this game, and it's too late for me to refund it, so now I'm stuck with it. Between this game, Fallout 76, the creator's club, and expecting us to pay full price for 10 different versions of Skyrim and counting, something is seriously wrong at Bethesda, and if they don't find a way to fix it, they may lose all of their customers. Stay far away from this one, folks.

Let me preface this by saying I have played The New Order, The Old Blood, and The New Colossus and thoroughly enjoyed all three games. The story is intensely immersive and one can get lost in the world of Wolfenstein very quickly.

Now...onto Youngblood. To say that I was hyped for another installment would be a gross understatement. I wanted to see the continuation of the story and was pumped for the new guns and fresh enemies. Needless to say the luster dulled up quick.

PROS:
--Superb gunplay as expected, some of the best in the FPS genre. 
--Visually stunning game.
--Fun continuation of the main storyline.
--Customization of weapons is improved.

CONS:
--Jess & Soph are extremely obnoxious protagonists and very unlikable.
--Levels are confusing and you can get lost in them VERY fast.
--Replayed levels over and over instead of new ones. Same level, just a different objective...yikes. 
--Enemies respawn in areas that you've already cleared.
--Enemy strength/level system immediately negates any well placed headshot or familiar tactic. 
--Microtransactions in a single-player game....JUST WHY?
--Main antagonists are generally uninspiring.
--Lack of BJ, the whole reason you play the game. You want to be Terror Billy!


BOTTOM LINE:
The rebooted Wolfenstein franchise has been an absolute grand slam in my opinion. A series that has flown under the radar when compared to other juggernauts in the FPS scene. Youngblood is a tragic misfire. I feel it was a rushed spinoff type game that really never felt like a true sequel. It's generally very frustrating to play and I hate to say it...but a complete waste of money. Here's to hoping that Wolfenstein III picks up where The New Colossus left off.

The first 2 games in the series were awesome. The direction they went with this installment is absolutely vile. Unnecessary grind padding so the game is longer than it actually is. Enemies have health bars effectively making them RPG damage sponges. Characters are shallow stereotypes with no interesting qualities whereas BJ is a pretty fleshed out character. Bad game design, low amount of content, cringe voice acting. In game store??? Game is just wack all around. The Wolfenstein minigame inside the game is better than the actual game.

Very disappointing entry to the Wolfenstein series. If you expect experience comparable to the previous 2 games you will be disappointed.

Game heavily leans into "open world" leveled type of RPG but without actual open world - few areas the game has are still separated by loading screens. This also means that some areas early on in the game will contain high level enemies that will just oneshot you, and that would be fine if sometimes for whatever reason you didn't have to go through those areas to complete lower level quests (although to be fair this issue becomes less and less common as you progress). This also means all enemies respawn regularly in the areas you've cleared, and due to an extremely limited number of areas you end up doing several different quests in the same exact areas several times over, which is ridiculous for a Wolfenstein game.

There is no new weapons and upgrades available for existing ones are really uninspired and typically come down to a game of number - you want slightly more damage or accuracy, etc.. Everything uses in-game currency to upgrade, which can be done 2 times per each component with only change being further stat increase but not appearance. At some point if you want to upgrade your arsenal more or less evenly it becomes just a tedious grind in your singleplayer/coop experience. But lucky for you game shop offers a solution - for a handful of coins you can buy timed XP boosts, currency boosts, health boosts, etc..

While a number of skins is available with in-game currency, almost every single one of them can also be bought with paid currency, and some can be only bought with in-game currency (arguably cooler ones).

If you are playing alone you're in for a ride - companion AI is extremely stupid and not really helpful. Your sister will often simplyfail to find a path towards you for a timely rez or get herself killed while being stuck looking for a path to you (while you are literally 5 steps away). AI also doesn't know how to deal with bosses at all, so it will just keep trying to shoot them in the face while following you, which becomes a problem on a particular boss (minor SPOILER!!!) that you need to shoot in the back. Overall playing with AI feels like a hindrance.

Story is quite uninspired, boring and short.

If you're looking for something like previous 2 games I would look elsewhere, you won't find it here. This game is an attempt at bringing in-game microtransactions into Wolfenstein franchise which is grotesque notion on it's own. Next thing you'll know they will be trying to nickel and dime you for every bit of content in the next Wolfenstein game.

Honestly I can't believe this game even has the Wolfenstein game name attached to it. Its terrible, everything bad you've heard about it is true unfortunately. I'm so bummed because I thought I would give the game a fair shake as I've loved all of the modern Wolfenstein games, however while this game on the surface looks like a Wolfenstein game, it does not in fact play like one. 

To be  honest this game plays a lot like a looter shooter (think Destiny) but without the loot and no incentive to keep going to level your character up as all the levels are reused over and over and over and over and over again for "different" side quests. Not to mention each time you come back to the area you "liberated" of Nazis, all the same exact Nazi's have respawned, making it a tedious nightmare to traverse levels. 

As far as characters, I like the idea of including female leads, however the game delivers this extremely poorly with flat characters that come off as weird and unlikeable. They have the most awkward one liners and jokes that make no sense to the audience. On top of which these two act more like the annoying side of frat bro culture than anything else, like the side everyone including other frat people probably detest. Its like whoever made these characters has never met a woman in a leadership position(s) or ever interacted with a sibling (the two main leads are supposed to be sisters but instead come off as weird lovers).

The worst part about it in my experience has been that the "Brother 3" level causes my and my friend's game to crash no matter how many things we have tried troubleshooting. Unable to finish the game and multiple hours in, the game will not stop crashing without even providing a reason for the crash. I want my money back and this is the first game I've actually said that for, however apparently it is against Steam policy to refund for a broken game that crashes if you are a few hours in. Note to all devs looking to make a buck, just make the first part of a game and don't finish it so the player gets just far enough in not to qualify for a refund. Probably saves a ton of money on development. Plus big name reviewer companies likely only play the first few hours before reviewing so you'll get at least an 8/10.

Long story short don't buy this game. Even if you are a huge Wolfenstein game, you will hate yourself for buying this game as it plays like a cheap knockoff. If you are looking for a co-op game to play with friends, still don't do it, there are so many better co-op titles out there that are more fun and don't regurgitate the same garbage mission after ever so tedious mission. Co-op in a Wolfenstein game could've been so cool, but this just ain't it.

Its maybe worth the price at $0, but perhaps even that is pushing it. Someone should pay you to play it, not the other way around.

This game… oh my God… I don’t even know where to begin. It’s nowhere close to the other Wolfenstein masterpieces. In short:

- Enemies are bullet sponges: entire magazines from the strongest weapons barely scratch the super ones.

- Bugs everywhere: supersoldiers can literally launch you into space (yes, flying out of the map is possible); enemies are randomly alerted or triggered, causing weird interactions even veterans don’t expect. Sometimes you get stuck on terrain for no reason and die instantly, and some rooftop spots force you to drop off the building. You can even get trapped under elevators, unable to move.

- After finishing the story, you can replay maps and change the difficulty. They call it “challenging,” but it’s a joke: enemies spawn right in front of or behind you, leading to instant deaths. They even spawn suicide dogs behind you that one-shot you.

- The game’s replayability sucks. It’s so boring—even for grinders like me who tried to get every achievement. You just replay the same scenarios hoping to do them faster, spending 15–20 minutes (at best) for one map, which nets only 16.000 XP and 800 gold—completely not worth the effort. Worth noting: if you stealth through a single section, you get 14.200 XP and 155 gold. So you earn almost the same XP for stealthing one easy section as you do for an entire mission!

- Weapon upgrades also require “improvements,” which cost money that’s hard to obtain consistently. The whole broken XP and gold system makes you question why you bought the game and what the creators were thinking.

- Nobody plays it. You might find one to three people in open lobbies. Otherwise, you’re stuck with an AI partner or need to rope in a friend.

- Certain parts of the map are locked and mission-specific, which is total nonsense. You may have completed that mission before, but when you replay the area those places are locked—often hiding loot you need.

- The final boss from the three-brother maps is a complete joke. No matter the difficulty, if you know where to hit it, it can be two-shotted. Yes, the FINAL BOSS can be TWO-SHOTTED.

- Cringe elevator scenes and dialogue that make you want to go to church.

- Worth mentioning: unlike previous Wolfenstein titles, you can only dual-wield pistols or SMGs—and only after you unlock the perk which doesnt make sense at all.

- The game keeps crashing with some “GPU problem” unique to this title. And if your internet connection drops for even one second, you’re kicked back to the main menu. When you reenter, you start at your last spawn.

Got every single achievement, closed the menu, and uninstalled the game off my PC. That alone should tell you everything. Zero stars. Would only recommend it to certified masochists—or anyone who thinks “being repeatedly fked in the a$$” is a fun weekend hobby.

I wanted to like this game but just can't, instead of just giving us more Wofenstein with Co-op as an option they force you to have to play with an AI. For the most part it stays out the way but its just annoying. Both sisters have shared lives which means if one of you goes down the other has to revive or you both lose a life. Not a bad idea if you have a human partner to play with, bad idea if you don't because you end up having to baby sitting the AI because if she goes down you have to revive her often in the middle of a damn fire fight surrounded by the enemy which will result in you going down also.

Then we have the change to gun mechanics, enemies now have different types of armor that go down faster with different types of guns.  Problem is if you run out of bullets in the middle of the fight now you have to switch to something less effective making the bad guys bullet sponges. So on top of having to baby sit the AI to keep you both alive you also have to juggle different guns at the same time. 

This all adds up to a game that is more annoying than fun to play. They took a winning formula from the other Wolfenstein games and mismashed in some things that don't make the game feel like the wonderful Nazi killing fest it was in the past. Only buy it if you have someone to play with. For solo players this is not the Wolfenstein you are looking for.

[h1]Disappointment for Wolfenstein lovers[/h1] but still enjoyable game.
[quote][b]Rating:[/b] 7.5/10[/quote]

Let's be clear. I LOVE the Wolfenstein series.  I loved every single one of these games, even the older ones. But let me tell you what's good and what's bad in this IMO, and then you can decide if you want to buy this. I'm going to review this with only 5 hours in-game spent.

[h1]The good:[/h1]
[list]
[*]1980's which means more over the top nazi/resistance technology
[*]The Wolfenstein Universe is expanded even further with casettes, VHS tapes and other cool collectible stuff
[*]Soundtrack is great as always
[*]The partner AI, is okay (I did not experience weird AI behavior)
[*]Gun customization
[*]The Plot (You can read. NO spoilers). I would say the plot is good. Nothing fancy, but it's convincing enough for me to believe that people would actually react in this way, if our reality were like this.
[/list]

[h1]The bad:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Insanely repetative and boring and let me explain why. This motherf....in' "progression system". I love a good rpg of this style like the Borderlands series, but man... This is soooo heavily nailed in the game, that you actually cannot do anything if you do not grind yourself to a higher level. Yes, this means that you have the freedom to go anyway you'd like(somewhat open world-ish), but you'll die anyway, if you go to a higher level zone. There are these campaign quests which are "level locked", meaning that you simply cannot finish them, if you do not meet the level requirement, as you simply get too much damage from them, and you deal too less to them. Bad game design. Don't get me wrong, I like grinding if it's fun. But sadly, this is not. It's basically farming the same "Dungeon" over and over again to level up. Sadly also these sidequests do not bring anything interesting to the table, so they are extremely boring to do. Go to point A. To this. Go back to HQ. And this goes on for a long time. This wouldn't be a problem, if you weren't forced to go through the same level over and over again. I understand that this "leveling up" mechanic makes sense for the girls, since they are not "experienced" enough to know everything. But overall, I don't feel like this was a good idea to add, or at least to add it, in this way.

[*]Level design looks good, but it get's old really quickly. It also does not enrich the Wolfenstein universe with it at all. These are just simple Parisian streets. (New Colossus had the level when you were at a city festival, New Order took you to the moon etc). The game offers some good things: 
 It runs super smooth, looks very sharp, doesn't put almost any real stress on my pc (gpu usage around 40-44%), and overall it's just a VERY well optimized game.
Also alt+tab works flawlessly which I appreciate a lot 🙂

 The style of environments, weapons and enemies is imo very cool, and aesthetically pleasing. Some smaller visual details, like your reflections visible in the windows, or your own full shadow are, let's say, positive nit picks 🙂

 The level design is also good, I like that they went with smaller, but multi layered maps with a lot of verticality; 
It's imo good playground for combat - and yet still looks like a city, not like an obvious arena dressed up with city decorations 🙂 

 Some coop gimmicks work pretty well - e.g. your AI companion can distract the bigger robot so you can blast it form the back 🙂 And overall I never had any problems with the AI ally, and for sure I was revived by my twin more times than the other way around.

Ok, now let's go with the bad and ugly 🙂
 There's a whole bunch of gameplay-design ideas that are either badly executed or total misfires even at theoretical level. 

The leveling system - how it was applied here imo - absolutely sucks.
 And for many reasons. 
 You gain levels and buy yourself abilities for points. Simple. A lot of these are pretty basic like more health, armor, ammo etc. But you can also unlock dual wielding or heavy weapons. 
 Fine, not over-complicated, it's "ok" ;p

What I dislike about it: 
 The arbitrary thresholds that don't let you buy what you want, even if you could afford it.
 For example I buy >bigger health< for 2 points, and I want to buy >even bigger health< since I still have points to spend. But I can't bc I need to reach 20th lvl first. 
 Imo this feels artificial, I already gained my points, just let me spend it for what I want, so I can lean into the playstyle I like. The game pretends that you have a choice, but constantly makes sure that you don't stray away from what the designers pre-scripted for you. 
 It feels like you're not progressing, but grinding in hamsterwheel of busywork just to keep up with the enemies (who also level up, but more on that later). 
 And It's not like YoungBlood is the only game ever guilty of that, this is a bigger trend started many years prior. It's still ass tho. 
 In good games, character progress isn't an afterthought slapped on pre-existing gameplay formula, but a core part of the formula itself. It should have a purpose, should let you lean into the things and skills you like etc, and should affect the gameplay in the process; 
 In many games released in the last +-10 years, character progress is like homework that you have to complete, just to close the gap between yourself and your leveling-up enemies, so the game will let you actually play the main part (which in this case is still mostly running and gunning, but now with extra steps).

It's similar with money;
 You collect coins, and can buy upgrades for guns. But these upgrades, even as basic ones as bigger magazine are locked until you reach certain level.
So for few hours you will constantly collect coins without having a chance to buy anything for them.

Gun upgrades are also bit nonsensical - bigger magazine gives you bonuses to damage and accuracy... Changing the gun's stock increases it's damage... Adding red dot sight increases firerate?
 Imo this is stupid.
 Good design is simple, intuitive and self explanatory. 
The bigger mag should give you a serious combat advantage just by itself. Better sight should let you headshot enemies from further away. Upgraded stock could just damp recoil a bit, etc. Clean, simple, somewhat logical. 
 Maybe some gamers just like to see how the numbers go up, but for me - subjectively speaking - guns aren't magic, and I like when the design matches with what the thing actually does. 
Here you have all these little bonuses to keep you busy with numbers, bc otherwise many players wouldn't even notice what's actually changes when you progress. 
 I bought every upgrade with damage bonus, hoping that it will cancel out the bulletspongy-ness of the enemies - fortunately it worked 🙂

So yea, imo both experience and currency systems are way off balance, not well thought out, don't interconnect well, and aren't anchored in the main gameplay loop - but are slapped on top of it as an afterthought.
 But they are mandatory if you want to progress and they keep u busy; 
So I guess the designers completed the task at hand and injected 'industry standard' solution into the game ;p 
I think 'manufactured complexity' is a good way to describe it.

What is also bad - enemies level-up with you. 
And because of that, your progress doesn't feel much like a progress at all. You get all these points, abilities and some bonuses like +2% damage once every few levels... but the bad guys are progressing with you, so after 5 hours of leveling up, you still have to dump a whole mag into a single trooper, just like in the very beginning. 
 Every time you level up, the game will match-up enemy levels to you, so you constantly fight against the bad guys who are your level or 1 level above.
 
 And when you roam around the semi-open hub levels, and you will hit the wall of very high level enemies that will be not only extremely bulletspongy, but also deal few times more damage than normal. 
 And they are the same soldiers, but with different number next to the healthbar. Which is imo another thing that comes off as very artificial and arbitrary.

Want some enemies to be much tougher than others? Design them as such.
Maybe make them bigger, attach more armor to them etc. Make it a logical part of the universe, so I can gauge the badguy's power by looking at him, not at his healthbar. 
 And sure, we have some enemies designed to be tougher and they look the part, but my problem is that the whole enemy roster constantly levels-up with you, making sure that you will never outgrow even the basic troopers. 

And the armor system in this game is... yet another arbitrary thing layered on top of the main gameplay loop, that exists only at the interface level and isn't reflected in the actual 3D assets of the enemies. 
So the enemies have 2 armor types, and the only thing that you can recognize it by, is the white squares/rectangles next to their healthbars. 
 
 You can face 2 (or more) copies of the same soldat, but one has rectangles next to the healthbar and the other one has squares.
 And now your job is to look at these rectangles/squares and choose the right ammo for the job. If you choose it wrong, the enemy is basically bulletproof. If you choose right, it will take 'only' 2 full mags from your SMG to put him down. And we're still talking about normal footsoldiers, game often throws much tougher enemy types at you, that require dumping many more mags full auto to destroy them. 

Imo after few hours this can really tire you out.
 Instead of powertrips with your big guns, you scroll through your arsenal and play rock-paper-scissors with your enemy's healthbars. After a while I just got used to it, and it wasn't as much of a problem as some reviewers like to suggest, but Its still NOT good (imo) gameplay idea, even at a conceptual level.

All these systems are like the interface-based meta-game layered over the actual 3D game itself. All these numbers, stats, levels, squares and rectangles work as their own thing detached from the world you see around you. So you just memorize these meta-rules and go along with them, bc otherwise you will die ;p

So even if the gameplay still has its good moments (and it has some) - imo they are swimming in the soup of busywork.

I wanted to like this game. I assumed the negative reviews were the typical, eye-rolling backlash that accompanies every game with female protagonists who aren't built like adult film stars. But Youngblood ended up being one of the worst first-person shooters I've ever played.


[b] STRUCTURE [/b] 

Structure is this game's cardinal sin. The previous Wolfenstein reboots were story-driven single-player experiences. They were set up like traditional story campaigns with beginnings, middles, and ends. Not so with Youngblood. Youngblood is a co-op mission-based game. It's meant to be played online, with a friend, in the style of something like Destiny. You fast-travel to various locations, complete objectives, fight enemies, and head back to the hub world. It's built around grinding for in-game currency to improve your weapons, unlock your skill tree, and buy cosmetic enhancements. There are also daily, weekly, and monthly objectives to meet, in the style of a free-to-play online shooter. The structure is a slap in the face to everything previous Wolfenstein games accomplished. It's impossible to find anyone to play with and has probably been that way since the first month of the game's release. I don't know why you would want to play with anyone anyway, because the missions [i] must [/i] be completed in one go. Saving and exiting means restarting the mission from the beginning. Dying three times also means starting the mission from the beginning. Not to mention, the missions are [i] excruciatingly [/i] long. You had better have two hours to commit, without interruption, every time you play. Otherwise, expect to repeat the same mission over and over. At the time of this writing, I've sunk eight hours into the game and have completed one - exactly [i] one [/i] - mission beyond the tutorial phase. I got to the final area of the mission, didn't realize it was the final area, exited the game for the night, only to discover there were no save points during missions, and I had to start over from the beginning. That one mission rocketed me to level 22 (because there's an RPG-style leveling system) and allowed me to unlock basically every tier-one weapon upgrade. One mission lasted almost as long as the entirety of The New Colossus. It's ridiculous the amount of time you're expected to invest in this slog.

[b] GAME PLAY [/b]

The game feels horrible. I can't sugar coat it. The series always struggled with weak-feeling guns, and these are the weakest yet. Enemies are bullet sponges. Since the game has an RPG-leveling system, your guns do damage based on your level. So headshots no longer kill standard enemies in one hit. Enemies absorb clip after clip, even on normal difficulty. (I started on hard, got annoyed with how tanky the enemies were, switched it to normal, and noticed no appreciable difference.) If stealth was overused in The New Colossus, it's rendered totally useless here. You have a cloaking device that allows you to move invisibly between enemies. But it drains in five seconds (before upgrades, which will take 25-50 levels to unlock) and only allows you to use a melee weapon. Since headshots no longer kill, it's impossible to eliminate an enemy with a gun, unnoticed, from cover, which makes the pistol a complete joke for the majority of the game. Nearly every encounter will lead to a firefight, and the enemies are always a few levels above you; so you'll always feel weaker than them. On top of that, the game introduces an armor mechanic that I don't understand. Some guns deal more damage to certain enemies, but I have no idea how to tell which enemy is weak to which gun. Armor is represented by little blocks beside their health bars. I can't tell the difference between heavy-armor blocks and light-armor blocks, and I don't know which gun damages which. It doesn't matter anyway, because guns frequently run out of ammo due to the bullet-sponge nature of the enemies. More than likely, you'll be shooting with whatever happens to be on hand. Word to the wise, don't invest too much in heavy weapons that you loot from elite and boss enemies. They run out of ammo in about three seconds and don't do much damage anyway. Say goodbye to the enemy-dissolving power of the Laserkraftwerk, or the face-melting fury of double shotguns. Nothing damages these Nazis.

[b] STORY [/b]

I can't comment much on the story, because I experienced almost none of it before I lost interest and stopped playing. The thing about Wolfenstein is that it was always carried by its characters. They were so full of color and personality compared to other titles. That's the missing ingredient here. The main characters are twin daughters of B. J. Blazkowicz, and they're either eleven or twenty-five years old. I can't tell. They look twenty-five, but they act eleven - slapping at each other, acting out Nancy-Drew-type detective stories, mimicking each other, etc. They have the ability to massacre thousands of Nazis, but they behave like kindergarteners. Maybe they mature as the plot develops. Maybe the story is trying to make a statement about child soldiers. I didn't get far enough to find out. And with the way the game is structured, I don't know how the story could have possibly progressed.

Aside from the Bazkowicz sisters, the rest of the cast is uninspired. There's a stereotypical girl-genius who can do anything and has no flaws. There are dull-as-dishwater resistance members who exist solely to give you quests. You won't find any wacky, haunted, or insightful characters here. Given the game's structure, I don't see how the plot could expand upon the abrupt ending of The New Colossus; so I guess that story remains a loose end forever. It's such a disappointment, taking the best narrative in the first-person-shooter category, sucking all the life out of it, and turning it into something that's practically a live-service model.

[b] CONCLUSION [/b]

I approached this game with optimism and ended up hating it. I thought it would reinvigorate the series, but it abandoned its winning formula entirely. It has all the previous games' flaws and none of their charm. If the Blazkowicz twins inherited the worst, most violent tendencies of their father, this game learned all the wrong lessons from [i] its [/i] parents. Its structure is atrocious. The multiplayer aspect, around which the entire game is built, is dead. It has no good characters, weak weapons, bullet-sponge enemies, useless stealth mechanics, and introduces grinding and leveling into a series that definitely didn't need them.

The one positive thing I can say about it is that it runs better on PC than New Colossus. Someone learned to optimize.

This is definitely the weakest entry in the rebooted Wolfenstein franchise. The story is, at its' high points a 6/10 but usually a 3/10, and gameplay is just ok which is surprising for a game on idtech 7. All they had to do was copy the mechanics over 1:1, and put them in the levels designed by Arkane. Which wasn't done. Speaking of which, the level design is the high point, probably an 8/10. But who cares about level design when the shooting you do in them doesn't fundamentally feel good?

There is a weapon upgrade system and an armor vulnerability system. I'll start off with the latter. I know some people dislike the health bars and armor vulnerability, but I think the health bars make sense. It's a co-op game, not singleplayer so it helps to know how many shots it'll take to kill off a particular enemy. So while it doesn't really fit in Wolfenstein, it's a necessary evil imho.

In regard to the armor vulnerability system, I think it's alright. Using the proper weapon to deal the right amount of damage isn't that big of a deal. However, time to kill is still too damn high, even with the proper weapon used on the right enemy. It's probably another side effect of being a co-op game, but it really does jack with how the game feels. Also, the most satisfying weapon in the game is dual-wielded machine-pistols. Yeah, that over the automatic-shotguns, Lasergewehr, and the AR. How.

Now for the weapon upgrade system. You get 3 different scopes, magazines, and other assorted upgrades per weapon, and you play the min/max game with them like an RPG. Here's my issue: the other Wolfenstein games give you weapons that feel good, and in Wolf II they give you two different fire modes that both feel good and have their own tactical use. Additionally, you can switch them in-game. In Youngblood, you play the min/max game to *make* your weapons feel good. They start off feeling like pea shooters and eventually evolve into "meh" versions of their Wolf II incarnation. Oh yeah, and you can't set two fire mods as favorites and switch between them on the fly. you have to go into the menu and tinker to get your weapon mods swapped. Even with the flashlight mod, which is necessary for some underground sections. Rather than just pressing your universal flashlight button, you need to go into your menu, swap to the flashlight mod for each weapon you want to use in the mission, press the flashlight button in-game again, and then you're set. It's Doom III all over again, but this design decision doesn't even make sense here since it's not going for that horror atmosphere. And the worst part? You need to switch that mod away once you're back on the surface so you can have your decently min/maxed weapons again.

One specific gripe I have is that the pistol, previously the dedicated stealth weapon, needs to be specc'd out (did I spell that right?) to feel right. Previously a one-tap headshot on all human enemies in other games, you now need the burst-fire mode to enable that functionality in addition to 3 weapon upgrades from the same company to enable higher headshot damage. Just... what? Locking basic fps mechanics behind an upgrade tree just doesn't feel good, especially coming from other Wolfenstein games which had elegant RPG-lite upgrade systems and weapons that were already really good in the first place.

And the worst part? This game helped turn me into one of those people who writes essay-length reviews. Damn it.

[h1]Wolfenstein: Youngblood - experiment that stuck between shooter and RPG?[/h1]

Although I played this game a lot I can't recommend it as a good game at least. And here's why:

[b]Gameplay and story[/b]

Devs added RPG systems in a linear classic shooter which don't work well with each other. You'll have a leveling system, where your stats increase each time to level up, as well as several skills you can acquire the more you increase in level. While this can make some shooters more diverse, in Wolfensteins case it is exactly the opposite. Here it's pointless since enemies scale with you, you'll never feel overpowered so why not simply just leave it as a normal shooter? To make matters worse, the whole idea of a Wolfenstein game was to be a toughguy and have fun while maintaining a balanced difficulty for some of us who enjoy a challenge but in Youngbloods case, enemies instead are given tons of armor and hp making them essentially bullet sponges. 

In W:Y you'll find enemies respawning or despawning behind you after you cleared or rushed a path or at times they'll just keep coming at you over and over. There's also no saving in the game unless you load a new zone which means if you plan on playing, pointlessly might I add, on higher difficulties, you'll most likely end up dying absurdly at some point later in the level and be forced to go through it all over again, essentially wasting at least an hour of your time. All these things are baffling and outdated gameplay mechanics/decisions that we have evolved from 10+ years ago.

The gunplay is amazing, if you played the previous Wolfenstein games you'll feel right at home when it comes to shooting Nazis in the head. There are also several weapon upgrades which you can unlock and they look great because they genuinely seem to affect the guns physically and visually.
When playing solo your AI sister is pretty much dead weight and considering there are no saves, you will essentially have to restart levels because it died or bugged. There are also microtransactions in a singleplayer game but they're pretty useless since you can end the game with your default skills and cosmetic equipment. Mostly they're fun to use if you're tired of using default skins and perks.

The story is set many years after the events of Wolfenstein 2, where the main character of the series, BJ, has settled down with Anya and their 2 daughters. The main events start after BJ disappears for no reason, and the 2 daughters are set on finding him by tracing his steps. The story of the game ends pretty stupid and makes no sense for series in general.

[b]Graphics and optimization[/b]

Regarding graphics the game looks exactly like the previous Wolfenstein game which is not a bad thing. Some locations can look really nice with some interesting Nazi sci-fi architecture. Sadly just like everything else in the game the scenes are ruined by being forced to go through them a lot of times over and over. There also doesn't seem to be any sense to how each level is tied to one another.
Performance although is great and I had no issues running this game on max settings as well as no major bugs encountered throughout the game. 

[b]Audio[/b]

The sound design overall is great, gun sounds and music are always fine. But I'd say voice acting of sisters is mediocre, and their jokes are like humour for 14 yo kids.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

If you're a Wolfenstein die hard fan then at some point on a huge sale I would say get it if you have a friend and don't have other awesome games to play at the moment. But if you simply want to play a coop shooter it's better to avoid the game and buy something from old Wolfenstein games.

I have now beaten this game both as a Singleplayer experience and as a Co-op experience and it's just such a let down compared to the previous Wolfenstein titles. A friend of mine recently played through the other Wolfenstein games, but didn't own this game, so I was happy to Co-op with them to avoid another copy of this dumpster fire being sold. I'll start off with some positives, graphically the game is fine and the gameplay itself is smooth and feels decent to play, but the biggest problem with that is the game itself is just a drag.

There's only 5 main story missions in Wolfenstein: Youngblood. The intro mission, Brothers 1, 2, and 3, and the final mission. The biggest problem with this formula is that mission 1 you start at level 1, then the brother missions all have a level entry of 20, and then the final mission you have to be level 32 to enter. This leads to a lot of unnecessary grinding that turns this 3-4 hour game into a 7 hour game because if you're even 1 level under leveled, you just get auto killed by literally every enemy in the game even if playing on the easiest difficulty. Leveling up doesn't do much to make you feel more powerful either because the enemies scale with your current level, so even though you'll be replaying the same areas over and over again, the enemies will always be at your level (or higher if you enter a mission with a level cap) so they all are just unnecessarily tanky and the fun movement and smooth gameplay just loses all momentum when you have to sit there and sink round after round into bullet sponge enemies.

The guns in this game might as well be Nerf guns. They tickle every enemy, and the AI seems to know they can tank hits because they just sit there and take it. The Tomahawk is probably the best weapon in the game because it's the only thing that can consistently 1 shot most enemies, though the game can be glitchy when it comes to picking them up which is always a pain. Enemies in this game can also stun you which is always a joy. Upgrading weapons doesn't seem to help much at all either because even with fully upgraded guns they hardly do anything to the enemies. The enemies also just randomly respawn with no rhyme or reason and you can't leave an area when the alarm is going off, so even if there's an enemy 100 meters away from you in game, you cannot use the metro to leave and often times led to frustrating moments of sitting and waiting for the game to decide there's no enemies left in the area, or just reloading the game to attempt to stealthily enter the metro since sometimes the game will dump you in an area with overleveled enemies that instantly kill you because of this game's garbage level scaling system.

A positive review? Hell yeah.

I played this cooperatively with a friend from start to finish which I believe was the way the game was intended to be played. We both went into this game reading and reflecting upon the negative reviews and so we had low hopes. Thinking it was not going to be fun and cringe. Expecting a huge grind that would make us tear our own luscious hair out their happy little pores.

Yeah, nah that wasn't our experience at all. We enjoyed the game from start to finish (on the hard difficulty). While there are some nitpicky things, the overall experience was positive. We laughed, we killed Nazis, we smirked and groaned at certain things in positive, negative and cringey fashion, but never did we feel like the game was holding us hostage to complete the story. Hell, we even did most if not all of the side missions.

The movement and gunplay? Fun overall. You have what is basically agile power armor and can zip around the map pretty quickly. I will say that on hard, you can get downed pretty quickly which I would say is to be expected. As you level up though you do get points to spend on suit upgrades so you know, it gets easier. We didn't max our characters when we finished the story, but we did look at some of the things and they seemed pretty neat.

The weapons all feel nice but you can only dual wield three types of weapons (pistol and two SMGs) which is kind of a shame but didn't really detract from the overall experience. There is a weapon upgrade/customization system that feels a tacked on as attachments just allow you to increase damage, accuracy, rate of fire while some upgrades may detract from another stat and if you have three from one category, you get a major buff to one of those stats but I believe you're only allowed at max, five customizations per gun? I could be a little incorrect, but that's mostly how it worked.

A few weapons can have a secondary unique attachment like an X-Ray scope for the assault rifle with such a niche use that I just switched back to a traditional optic. Some attachments can also change how a weapon behaves. Like shooting slow projectiles that do more damage. Changing the explosive shot from a weapon to do perform as a cluster bomb. A flashlight (because your suits don't have one). Having your gun maybe do something as the secondary. All in all, it's neat and can help players mix up their gameplay a little if they so wish.

One silly thing is you can purchase (with in game money) suppressors for some guns which would supplement stealth gameplay...except enemies have health bars and there really isn't a one hit kill with pistols for example...so it just turned into "shoot them a lot before their alert meter goes up" which we found hilarious AND ridiculous. Players do eventually unlock the ability to one-hit certain enemies with throwables and you can do stealth melee kills but performing the formers? Hilarious. 

I will also note that we were not fans of enemies having light and heavy armor and each weapon their own affinity for what armor they're proficient at destroying. Certain enemies can have their armor chewed through regardless of what armor as it basically turned into a DPS thing, but we just wanted to use a gun and pew pew. Was annoying having to see enemy armor mid-fight and switch to another gun.

The RPG-style health for enemies was basically of no source of contention for us. In the early part of the game, we did attempt to do some missions that were way above our pay grade, and we learned quickly to not do that again. While yes that is "not a normal Wolfenstein gameplay mechanic", this isn't a "normal Wolfenstein game". So we just did missions at or close to our level, got on with our gameplay session. If you don't like that style, aite.

The protagonist sisters? Quirky, funny, and a little cringe but not in anyway that detracts from the game at all. In fact, we both loved the elevator camera loading scenes. We both wish there were more. Their banter wasn't annoying to us at all. In fact, nothing about the protagonists bothered us at all.

Graphics and performance are good as well. There's definitely a lot less destructible things in the world but the game runs pretty smooth. We did get an occasional crash. Maybe once every two or three game-sessions but it was usually on their end, who was using the Buddy Pass. I myself maybe experienced one or two? 

If we had to complain about anything else, it would probably just be the keybinds and maybe how some things activate. If felt a little clunky with dual-wielding and operating the flashlight while dual-wielding. The only other thing would be the sound of the other player's footsteps while running. They are hilariously mismatched in tempo from what you hear versus the player.

[b]Nostalgie mit Terror Billy[/b]

Let's do some backtracking first, shall we? When [i]New Order[/i] came out in 2014 it was a nice surprise. Also, it was the first of the classic [i]id Software[/i] IPs to get a new version. We were 2 years away from [i]Doom[/i] and had to wait 3 years for [i]Quake Champions[/i]. These games also had multiplayer while these new Wolfenstein games are solely made for a single player experience. What's more is that the developer is not [i]id Software[/i] but a Sweden-based company called [i]MachineGames[/i].

Having a new, alternate history taking place in the '60s (getting rid of the '40s once and for all) was a great idea and the many cutscenes and the good voice-acting did their job. Dual-wielding was fun and stealth-based sequences (not always preferring the mayhem solution) where commanders were present was a novelty in this franchise. Not many people like [i]New Colossus[/i] but I think it was even better. Overall, this is the premise I had and then decided to pick up the story in [i]Youngblood[/i].

[b]Kumpelpaß[/b]

Let's get this out of the way first. I was trying to play the game with the so-called [i]Buddy Pass[/i] 2 years ago upon its release but it didn't work properly. Should you purchase the Deluxe version with this feature you can invite a friend to play together. But your friend cannot obtain achievements and no statistical data (progress) will be saved for them. Just purchase the game - it is heavily discounted nowadays and the regular version will suffice to the both of you. I noticed the Bethesda launcher is not needed if the purchase is made via Steam. 

[b]Kooperatives Gameplay[/b]

The new addition a lot of people feared but it arrived: cooperative gameplay. Take it or leave it! The A.I. is overall good. It picks you up quickly if you're down and until you engage in combat it stealthily moves around. Expect boss battles to be tough as the A.I. does not recognise that using a heavier weapon against bigger enemies would be better. If you want to do some search for missed collectibles or some additional side missions head in alone otherwise I recommend that you complete the story with a friend. Much better to experience the game this way.

[b]Geschichte[/b]

The story is what makes this game a huge letdown. The girls are not as badass as their father is. That's fine, they're growing up. The idea here is to go against orders coming from high up as they decide to look for their dad as soon as they find out he is MIA. The problem with [i]Youngblood[/i] is that it only offers 6 (!!!) missions. That's 6 different locations. Yes, they are varied and Neu-Paris looks amazing but this is nothing compared to previous episodes. The antagonist is not as memorable as Irene Engel and there is too much focus on looking for B.J. instead of looking at the big picture: What are the Nazis planning? This is the '80s, they have lost a lot of areas already, the resistance is gaining on them. And what about Da'at Yichud? I want to know more! Remember the scene with Irene on the train or the strawberry milkshake in the diner? No such amazing cutscene here, nothing!

[b]Fähigkeiten und Waffen[/b]

The girls level up and acquire skill points. You purchase abilities and you make those better. One particular is story-related and hidden and some are not well-positioned and are a must as soon as you can obtain them. Heavy weapons (the so-called hammer items) can only be part of your inventory if you acquire the corresponding skill. Now, the girls already wear high-tech armor so you'll appreciate the ability to cloak. It helps the stealth-based gameplay but should you be spotted a lot of enemies will attack you. 

The so-called [i]kraftwerk[/i] weapons can be used to enter new areas by making doors explode or electrocute a forklift to activate its forks that opens up a garage-like secret area. Dual-wielding returns but not available for the shotguns or the rifles just for the machine gun and the pistol. You collect coins to be able to upgrade your weapons. Components have their improved versions. You can increase the fire-rate or have the supercharge function for your favourite weapon. Have a different scope or install a flashlight as several locations can be found underground! An interesting concept I welcomed but the RPG elements remain minimalistic in a primarily action-oriented game.

[b]Nebenmissionen und Aktionen[/b]

[i]New Colossus[/i] already employed some side missions to increase the longevity of the game. [i]Youngblood[/i] tries to improve upon them as the tasks are given by your friends in the HQ area (which is in the catacombs of Paris). Some open up new sections on levels you already explored but you will still feel cheated about the short campaign experience. A new side mission type is introduced - so-called actions that are given to you by Abby. These are ad-hoc missions that can only be completed while you're on the spot. Plant a bomb in a parked car nearby, kill a commander, steal an enigma machine, plant a listening device etc. Locations vary even for returning actions. You also have challenges that change on a daily and weekly basis. Just talk to Abby in HQ and you can also replay story missions if you want. 

[b]Das schlechte Zeug[/b]

I have to add a separate section for the bad stuff as there are some in this game. I already mentioned the story which is a huge letdown following [i]New Colossus[/i]. The girls some people like some don't. They are not B.J., accept it. Side missions and actions are varied and many but they do not make up for the story. There is a huge (and I mean huge) amount of collectibles. For the first time in a video game I felt they were too many. 3D glasses, journals, letters, concept arts, floppy discs, VHS cassettes. Some are very well hidden - once you pick the ability that shows them on your minimap things will get much easier.

Now, enemies tend to respawn. That's fine but not when they do it right in front of you. You'll die a lot. This is irrespective of your experience in FPS games. Are you good at making headshots? Doesn't matter. Light and heavy armor are introduced. First you need to remove these and only then can you really hurt your Nazi foes. The lower-right corner of the screen shows if the weapon you're holding is good against that particular armor. If not, you need to change otherwise taking out a [i]Zerstörer[/i] heavy robot will take eternity.

The game has no extra content. Nothing. A free update introduced some treasure hunting which is good for levelling up fast but that's it. All your weapons and the girls' armor have different skins. The majority you purchase with your coins but some require gold. This you won't find in the game - you need real money to purchase them. Microtransactions were never famous and [i]Youngblood[/i] ensures they will remain so.

[b]Mein Urteil[/b]

I have mixed feelings when it comes to the latest installment in this series. I always loved the story and [i]Youngblood[/i] gives us something that is nowhere near acceptable. Coop can be a hit-and-miss with an A.I. and the game has a lot of achievements that require grinding. This is for weapon masteries, upgrades and obtaining all skills. You can do 100% (collectible-wise) on a save and you will still miss a few of the 'cheevos nearing 50 hours. 

What saved the game for me (and upvoting it instead of the opposite) is the gameplay. It is great as usual and I spent a lot of time walking around cloaked taking down Nazi officers silently. The locations are as detailed as you'd expect and the '80s vibe is also there. Listening to cassette tapes and finding out what '80s action flick they made fun of by having their German equivalent is good for some laughs. 

Pick it up if you're a fan of the (new) series but don't expect a good story just a great gameplay.

I genuinely don't know what happened here. Somewhere along the way, this franchise went from producing games that actually justified the excitement surrounding them to delivering something that feels like it was designed to be played in five-minute bursts on a phone while you're waiting for your food to arrive. And somehow, despite having the gameplay depth and overall appeal of a mobile game, it manages to run like you're trying to play Cyberpunk 2077 on a GTX 1050 Ti while your PC is being held together with duct tape and a desperate prayer.

Honestly, that's an impressive achievement in its own right. Not a good one, mind you, but an achievement nonetheless.

The biggest problem is that this game doesn't just fail to live up to the franchise's legacy; it feels like it barely understands what made that legacy worth having in the first place. Previous entries established a certain standard, and you'd reasonably expect a new installment to at least attempt to meet that standard. Instead, this feels like someone looked at everything fans enjoyed about the series, threw most of it out the window, and decided that whatever remained was good enough to slap the franchise's name on.

Apparently, brand recognition is now a substitute for quality.

The gameplay feels shallow, the overall experience lacks the substance you'd expect, and the whole thing gives off the impression that it was designed around the question, "What's the absolute bare minimum we can get away with?" rather than "How do we make something worthy of this franchise?" Every time you start to think there might be something worthwhile underneath the surface, you're reminded that you're playing a game that seems far more interested in occupying your time than rewarding it.

And then there's the performance.

Oh, the performance. What a spectacular mess.

Imagine taking a game with the apparent complexity of a mobile title and somehow making it run like a technically ambitious, graphically demanding PC game from the future. You'd think the developers had accidentally left an entire second game running in the background, except that would imply there was enough substance here to justify those hardware demands in the first place.

Comparing this experience to Cyberpunk 2077 running on a GTX 1050 Ti might sound unfair to Cyberpunk, and honestly, it probably is. At least Cyberpunk has the excuse of being an enormous game with a detailed world, complex systems, and a tremendous amount happening on screen. When that game struggles on underpowered hardware, you can at least understand why. Here, you get to experience performance problems without the corresponding benefit of feeling like you're playing something particularly impressive.

It's like being charged the price of a luxury sports car for the privilege of driving a shopping cart with one square wheel. Sure, you're technically moving, but at some point you have to wonder why you're putting up with the experience at all.

And before anyone rushes in to explain that performance can vary depending on hardware, settings, drivers, or whatever other perfectly reasonable technical explanation might apply, let me clarify something: optimization is part of the product. I shouldn't have to become an unpaid technical support engineer just to make a game that feels like a mobile title run acceptably. If a game is going to demand the patience of a NASA engineer to operate, I'd at least appreciate it doing something impressive once it's running.

The most frustrating part is that this is a franchise with an established history. There's a foundation to build on. There are previous games to learn from. There are fans who already know what the series is capable of. This isn't some brand-new experimental indie project where a few rough edges are understandable. This is an installment that has the benefit of everything that came before it, yet somehow manages to feel like a downgrade in both ambition and execution.

That's what makes the disappointment sting. If this were an entirely new IP, I might shrug, call it mediocre, and move on. But when a franchise has previously demonstrated that it can do better, watching it settle for something this underwhelming feels less like a creative misstep and more like a complete failure to understand its own audience.

Naturally, there will be people who enjoy it. There are people who enjoy just about anything, and good for them. If you're having fun, I'm not going to tell you that you're wrong. But enjoyment doesn't magically erase the technical problems, make the gameplay deeper, or turn an underwhelming sequel into a worthy successor. Sometimes a disappointing game is just a disappointing game, no matter how many people insist that you're supposed to appreciate it for what it is.

And that phrase, "appreciate it for what it is," is doing an awful lot of heavy lifting here.

What it is, as far as I'm concerned, is a disappointing entry in a franchise that deserves better. It's a game that seems content to coast on the reputation of its predecessors while delivering an experience that feels considerably cheaper, shallower, and less polished than it should. The fact that it can simultaneously feel like a mobile game and perform like it's trying to render the entire universe in real time is almost comical. Almost.

If you're a longtime fan of the franchise, I would strongly recommend tempering your expectations. Then temper them again. And after that, maybe lower them a little further, just to be safe. Going in expecting the quality of previous entries is a recipe for disappointment, and I wouldn't recommend spending your money on the assumption that the franchise name guarantees anything resembling the experience you remember.

As for the negative reviews, I'd take them seriously. Normally, I like to form my own opinions rather than letting reviews dictate what I play, but sometimes the collective wisdom of people who have already spent their time and money on something is worth listening to. In this case, the warnings are worth considering before you make the same mistake.

There are plenty of games out there that respect your time, justify their hardware requirements, and actually build upon what made their predecessors successful. This doesn't feel like one of them.

My recommendation: Trust the bad reviews, save your money, and don't waste your time.

If you're looking for a worthy continuation of the franchise, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a polished, well-optimized experience, look elsewhere. And if you're looking for something that justifies the excitement surrounding its release, you might want to look somewhere else entirely.

At this point, revisiting one of the older games sounds like a much better use of your time. At least then you'll be reminded why you liked this franchise in the first place, rather than spending hours wondering how it managed to fall this far.

What a disappointment. The franchise deserved better, the fans deserved better, and frankly, my hardware deserved better.

Save yourself the headache. Read the negative reviews, believe what they're telling you, and move on.

Just a note for this review. I played all the modern Wolfenstein games back to back, from The New Order to Youngblood, just to properly experience the whole series, but I am reviewing each game separately.

What an oddball this game is. On one hand it tries really hard to present itself as a proper Wolfenstein game, not just because it has the name, but also because the story takes place years after The New Colossus. On the other hand it feels completely flat, like a stitched together patchwork of half baked ideas that were never fully developed. It feels like they tried many different things at once, left back doors open for each idea and in the end did not fully commit to any of them.

First of all the story. It feels more like a side quest than a proper continuation and when you finally find out why Blazkowicz disappeared, the explanation feels completely out of character and honestly nonsensical, even the twist with the main villain was just silly, to put it politely. That said, after playing the previous installment, nothing story wise can really disappoint me anymore in this franchise. One small caveat I have to add though... I have seen many people complain about the two main characters and their "HELL YEAH DUDE" dialogue, but honestly you are playing as two teenage girls, they are supposed to be insufferable by nature, so at least that part was technically accurate.

Gameplay, gunplay, and overall design choices also feel very strange. One of the strongest parts of the previous game was the combat. Guns felt great, enemies finally had real weak spots and even on the highest difficulty it did not turn into a bullet sponge fest. This game completely reverses that with the added level system. If enemies are a higher level than you, good luck killing them without dumping all your ammo or barely surviving the encounter. That said, I do prefer the weapon upgrade system here. It feels more polished and offers a bit more variety, which is one of the few clear positives.

I do not mind a non linear structure like this game uses, but it feels extremely grindy. You are constantly replaying the same stages with different objectives, but nothing really changes. Maybe you take a slightly different path, maybe enemies are placed a bit differently, but that is about it. You can clearly feel the moment when you finish the prologue and unlock the mission board. This is where Arkane influence is very obvious. The hub based mission structure, reused maps, and objective driven level design feel straight out of Dishonored / Prey / Deathloop. I mean it is not bad, but it just does not fit a Wolfenstein game at all.

Oh and did I mention this game forces coop? You cannot truly play solo or offline. The second character is always controlled by an AI. I have no idea what the original intent was with this game or what they were trying to achieve, but it ends up feeling incomplete and confused, without a clear identity, just like multiple different games stitched together.

If you get it heavily discounted it might be okay-ish, especially if you want to play it with a friend. But I really cannot recommend it in general. Even if this was a standalone game not associated with Wolfenstein at all, it would still be a huge "meh" experience that tries to fill its gaps with boring grind.

I really tried to love this game, I bought all the franchise since New Order, Return to Castle, Wolfenstein (the one that cannot be bough anymore) and a few others, and I'm a true fan of the franchise. BUT.

1. The most important aspect of why I don't like this game is this: it was designed from the ground up to slowdown the game and maximize the time the player will spend within world in whatever tedious way exists. That doesn't seem too bad isn't? Well, it is the worst. YOU CANNOT SAVE, THERE IS NO CHECKPOINTS (except a few, one per main mission, top). So, that means that a 1h30 play will have to be restarted from the beginning when you get to the climax of the final battle. Yeah, that's no fun at all, in particular because to get there some really difficult battles have happened. And when you restart the level, you don't restart from your previous save, you return to basically the state when you died, probably without ammo, shared lives, etc, and now you have to deal with all the enemies again with nothing on you. Killing a giant robot with the pistol? Check. Yeah, there is no way to kill a giant robot with the pistol, even with full ammo, and yeah, hitting it in the right places.

But also there are other details:

- Having to break a box to get loot with the axe takes like 10 hits in different parts of the box.
- Meaningless collectibles EVERWHERE so you have to stop playing and search every little corner for every damn collectible.
- And the worst, this side actions that appear in a level after a mayor battle, so you have to go to a different part of the map, do some meaningless chore, and return back to find the mayor battle enemies have re-spawned. Now, low on ammo, and without a save, you have to repeat what you just did YET AGAIN. And remember, DON'T YOU DARE TO DIE.

2. There is no story. There is a hint of a story, but nothing compare to the beautiful and complex story of the New Order or the New Colossus. It feels basically like an barebones Wolfenstein engine that can be played in co-op, nothing more. There is no story on how we got here after the New Colossus, how the girls were raised, what happened to the world, why Blazkowicz stopped fighting the Nazi, what happened to the Nazi regime after Hitler got killed, really nothing. Adding to the above, for example, in the New Order the supersoldiers were introduced by a cut scene. Here, I find gigantic robots as nothing special at all. Remember how you got the LaserKraftWerk in The New Order? With the mini-puzzle and all, in a research lab? Well, here it is sitting in a dirty office as it was nothing and with a half-backed dialog.

They are cartoonish version of an angry teenager with all the stereotypes in. But they are not the only ones, for example the resistance members. Remember Fergus Reid, Seth Roth or obviously Max Hass. I almost cried when Max seem to be killed saving others. Here, really, they are a bunch of NPCs stereotypes.

4. Weapon upgrades are mostly useless. In the New Colossus weapon upgrades really did a difference and had strategic uses. LKW had the supercharge, which allowed to hit a boss with all the charge of this weapon, and then continuing the battle with something else. In Youngblood, all upgrades are basically ways to balance accuracy, rate of fire and damage. That's it.

5. Crashes and memory leaks. My girlfriend with a Nvidia RTX2060 had to restart the game at each reload, because the game will consume all graphic memory and started to freeze.

6. Yeah, killing Nazi is fun, but it quickly becomes tedious if there is nothing supporting the engine.

Wolfenstein Youngblood is far from the game you are expecting or were hoping for from the franchise, but is it bad?

Surprisingly, no. I was very anxious when I initially got the entire modern reboot series on steam, including this one. Its staggeringly offputting "mostly negative" rating made me think that this was going to be an IP destroying flop, only to find out that it actually sold very well and was one of the best selling retail games in the UK and Japan, ever. Not only that, overall, most people hate it for the fact you do not play B.J and its clear people were wanting, earnestly, a true sequel. 

The virtual reality game, Cyberpilot, got the same treatment. The studio is obviously a bit fatigued with the high value, cinematic, singleplayer games and were also obligated to shift focus on the Doom reboot series, as well as make some gimmick games to keep the IP alive. The VR game and co-op game, this one, are the obvious results of the 'necessary evils' that come with being a major developer in this industry. 

But Youngblood, even though it does act as a direct continuation of Wolfenstein II, as well as playing into one of the last unexplained story hooks from its conclusion, was never marketed as being the be-all, end-all conclusion of the Wolfenstein trilogy. We know now, that Wolfenstein III is coming and it was not Youngblood. We have no idea if it will be immediately before Youngblood, during or after, but overall, Youngblood is certainly an overhated game for almost no reason. 

It definitely is a bit grindy, but you can get a remarkably good single player experience on lower difficulties and the co-op AI is actually pretty competent. In the end, I only did a few other side missions besides the necessary ones that assist greatly in the main ones, which still barely brought me past the six hour mark. One extra hour of my playtime exists merely because I had paused a mission and made dinner. All around, this is a game that can be beaten competently in a single sitting session. But it can also, easily, become a dozens or more hour game with the amount of side missions and co-op shenanigans that can be afoot.

Honestly, this game does have some story and the cutscenes are sadly, not up to snuff of the series' incredible and well known pre-rendered cutscenes. But overall, the humour is there and seeing what became of some characters, actually is pretty interesting. 

The gameplay is very un-Wolfenstein like, but honestly it definitely felt more like Old Blood's never ending waves of infantry. A lot of the complaints regarding the gunplay and bullet sponge-enemies exist fully in the base games as well. My biggest complaint (which is still a minimal one) about the Wolfenstein reboot series overall, is that it has some of the best gunplay in any game and it unfortunately devolves into straffing around bullet-sponge enemies with machine guns, which considerably kills the pace and at times, robs you of the momentum we see in the Doom reboots. 

So while this game is not narratively as strong and B.J's kids, the Terror Twins, are somewhat intolerable at first, it is hard not to like everyone a little tiny bit, if not just because they do grow gradually, just enough, to reveal they do in fact have personalities beyond their archetypes. Honestly, this game is definitely an experiment in minimalism in many factors because it was meant to be played between two people, who are in frequent communication. 

So, if you come into it as a singleplayer Wolfenstein experience, you may be disappointed, but I think the co op aspect, the way it is meant to be played, is very competent. 

I like the prep system a lot and I think that even though the gore has been toned down a bit, there is still great satisfaction with how it feels breaking into a Nazi lady's office and then rendering her sunglasses-clad corpse limbless as pools of blood stretch into her personal study. Her dead, Vichy-Fascist Frenchie guardsman being organically reassembled to act as entrail and gib-decorations around her entire flat. 

The hub movement and some of the mission dynamics reminded me of Homefront: The Revolution, a game that I actually enjoyed a lot that is also overhated. In the end, these games are best bought on sale for cheap and with full awareness of what experience you are walking into. You don't have to do every single little mission, nor should you, the game truly lasts as long as you want it at a certain point. 

It is interesting to see what decades of German occupation has done to France. Croissants are no longer publicly available, German upper class nobles have guilty pleasures like sushi rolls and of course, every other city block is a cigarette advertisement, a cafe, an exhibition for some major movie and finally, a bavarian pretzel diner. Meanwhile, deep in one of the Brother towers, we see Vichy-fascists continue to eat their croissants in silence. 

There is a huge potential here for the next game, a Vichy France setting is so unique and unexplored, considering the absolute willingness of the real life, short lived Vichy regime and the fact its own harshness surprised even the Germans, Wolfenstein Youngblood finally indulges us in one of humanity's greatest fantasies, fighting the French. And of course, the French Nazis being wine swigging, turncoat partisans, noble blooded collaborators and generally just terrible people, makes for the gameplay to be entirely guilt free. 

However, most of the forces you face are still going to be German. Even the Vichy coded troops are speaking German. It almost implies that French itself has been eradicated as the lingua franca, ironically. 

The hub world is pretty cool, taking place in the Paris Catacombs. The French Resistance is realistically portrayed as a multi-skilled, multi-ideological partisan effort composed of not only those resistance to fascism, but actual communists, including an outright Soviet. This is always something that the reboot series has gotten flak for, the presence of radical leftists and outright, revolutionary socialists among the resistance groups. But this is a hard coded reality of these groups in history. 

The Nazis had made themselves the sworn enemies of Bolshevikism and had ordained themselves as the vanguards against the "Communist conspiracies" along with a certain other group of politically prevalent individuals. It was only natural that communists and all sorts of leftists, also Christians, rival fascists and rival monarchists, even liberals and reluctant reformers, would align themselves with the distinction of being fascism's eternal enemy, as fascism had already dictated this for them.

And honestly, if the politics of the game bother you, why? Rightists and Leftists continuously engage with content made by people who hate and demonize them. Its usually the boneless liberals that get insanely and utterly mad at there being anything related to either extreme of the spectrum, while liberals themselves cannibalize talking points from both. But I suppose it is better than reactionary pouting or socialist sabre rattling. At least those guys have an aesthetic.
